title: scheduler-pulse-latency-forensics
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a focused set of experiments that we ran to isolate and reduce rare P99+ spikes caused by poor coalescing behavior in continuous batching. This doc is rough — aiming to capture the probing methodology (the "pulse" idea), the profiling artifacts we used to attribute time to queue/scheduler/kernel stages, and short ladder of mitigations to iterate on.

Why this felt necessary:
- Multiple SRE incidents in May/June where P99.9 jumps for certain tenant mixes (small requests with interleaved long-seq requests).
- Existing adaptive timeouts reduce average latency but leave odd long tails that are hard to reproduce.
- We saw multiple handoffs between queueing, scheduling, and kernel dispatch that align with the tails. Need clearer breakdown.

Pulse technique (high level):
- Instead of only sweeping static timeouts/batch-size, we inject short intentional "flush pulses" into the scheduler to force batches to be emitted at controlled offsets and measure the downstream cost of partial batches on the tail distribution.
- Rationale: natural arrival rhythm can mask interactions; pulses let us generate edge-case microtraces deterministically.

Hypotheses we tested:
1) Tail spikes are correlated with repeated preemption of a coalesced batch by a higher-urgency microburst arriving after kernel dispatch is scheduled but before GPU execution starts.
2) Small partial batches hitting kernel scheduling boundary cause disproportionate setup/teardown overheads (CUDA context, cuBLAS warmup) that amplify tails.
3) Priority demotion rules occasionally starve older requests because the demotion thresholds align poorly with batch-formation windows.

Experiment plan and workloads:
- Controlled workload generator (local harness): mix of 80% short prompts (10 tokens), 20% long prompts (1024 tokens). Interarrival distribution = Poisson with adjustable lambda + periodic 100ms "pulse" insertion.
- Nodes used: 2x p4d-like test rig (8x A100 emulation), single-tenant and 3-tenant multi-tenant mixes.
- Scheduler builds instrumented: patch branch pulse-experiments (see PR), add per-request lifecycle timestamps: enqueue_time, slot_assigned, batch_formed, flush_sent, kernel_dispatch, kernel_start, kernel_end, response_sent.

Key config knobs we swept (examples):
- flush_timeout_ms: 3, 6, 12, 25
- min_batch_size: 1, 4, 8, 16
- urgency_decay: 0.1, 0.25, 0.5
- preemption_grace_ms: 0, 8, 20
- kernel_dispatch_window_ms: 0, 2, 5

Observability & tooling used:
- microtrace collector (trace IDs attached to requests from harness)
- NVTX annotated traces + cupy/nvprof captures for kernel timeline (sampled 1/1000 requests)
- Flamegraphs for userland scheduler threads (perf, pprof)
- Custom python analyzer that computes per-stage latency and emits waterfall CSVs for each trace
- Prometheus metrics: batch_size_distribution, flush_reason (timeout|size|pulse), preempt_count, kernel_wait_time_ms

Representative findings:
- When pulses are aligned with scheduler flush_timeout (same order of magnitude), we get clear cohorts of partial batches that show kernel_wait_time spike: warmup+context switching adds ~1.1-1.6ms overhead per partial batch on our test nodes.
- P99 for short requests reduced from ~82ms to ~56ms when we add a 2ms kernel_dispatch_window that batches dispatch attempts arriving within that window. Median unaffected.
- Preemption_count correlates strongly with P99.9. Configs with preemption_grace_ms > 8 reduced P99.9 by ~18% in multi-tenant mixes.
- Urgency demotion parameter mis-tuning: using a hard decay (0.25) caused starvation in cohort where many small requests keep being demoted; switching to additive urgency reduction (fixed -0.05 per second) smoothed tails.

Example microtrace (excerpt, humanized):
- req A (short): enqueue 0ms, slot_assign 3ms, batch_formed 6ms, flush_sent 6.5ms, kernel_dispatch 6.9ms, kernel_start 7.2ms, kernel_end 9.5ms, response 10.1ms
- req B (short, same batch): enqueue 1ms, slot_assign 3ms, batch_formed 6ms, flush_sent 6.5ms, kernel_dispatch 6.9ms, kernel_start 7.2ms, kernel_end 9.5ms, response 10.2ms
- req C (long, high priority arrives late): enqueue 5.8ms, forces preempt at 6.4ms -> batch A/B preempted (kernel dispatch delayed), req A/B kernel_wait increases to 12ms, total response jumps -> tail

Profiling hotspots (userland):
- scheduler thread: lock contention spikes when batch formation scanning touches many small queues (contention on queue-metadata).
- dispatch path: serialization of the kernel descriptor building step under one mutex (we have a TODO in code to split descriptor create).
- GC/allocs: small ephemeral vectors allocated during batch concatenation account for 4–6% of time in high churn experiments.

Mitigations attempted and results:
1) kernel_dispatch_window (coalesce dispatch attempts within N ms) -> reduced micro-preemptions. +2ms window = best tradeoff on p99 with small median cost.
2) relaxed preemption (grace period) -> eliminated pathological immediate preemptions at the cost of slightly longer queues for urgent jobs; net P99.9 improved in multi-tenant tests.
3) split descriptor creation into per-thread pools (reduced lock contention, cut that stage by ~30%).
4) fallback fast-path for single-request batches (skip some concat logic) -> reduced median by ~1.4ms but increased cpu by small amount.

Failure modes and tradeoffs observed:
- Increasing dispatch_window reduces tail but buffers urgency: urgent long requests may wait a bit longer. Need safety SLA for high-priority clients.
- Reducing preemption increases latency for high-priority arrivals if they truly need immediate execution. Balance via tiered preemption (only allow preempt for tier >= X).
- Fast-paths introduce code complexity and can regress under heavier GPU contention (we saw a minor throughput dip at very large batch sizes).

Action items (next iteration):
- [ ] Formalize pulse harness and add to perf/regression suite (Ethan) (JIRA ENG-4821)
- [ ] Add NVTX sampling flags to production tracer so we can correlate kernel_wait_time to real incidents (Daniel)
- [ ] Implement descriptor pool split and land small PR (María) -> bench again with mixed-tenancy
- [ ] Design safe tiered preemption policy and run cost/latency racks tests (Priya)

Open questions / notes to discuss on call:
- Is a dynamic dispatch_window (based on current qlen and GPU busy ratio) preferable to static? early tests show it might be stable but risk oscillation.
- Should we expose a new tenant-level SLA flag: allow_burst_preempt (boolean) so enterprise customers can opt in?
- Where to set acceptable tradeoff: reduce P99 vs. protect 99.999 for urgent SLA tenants.

Appendix (raw numbers snapshot):
- baseline (flush_timeout 12ms, min_batch 4): P50=22ms, P95=42ms, P99=82ms, P99.9=210ms
- dispatch_window 2ms, preemption_grace 8ms: P50=23ms, P95=40ms, P99=56ms, P99.9=174ms
- dispatch_window 5ms, preemption_grace 20ms: P50=25ms, P95=45ms, P99=60ms, P99.9=160ms

Notes to self (scratchpad):
- reproduce a single-tenant version that still shows tail (if so, kernel warmup likely major).
- consider microbenchmark: repeated 1-request kernel dispatch vs grouped multirequest to get warmup amortization numbers.
- look at GPU SM occupancy when tiny batches hit to quantify warmup cost.

References / links: JIRA ENG-4821 (work to track), PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/778, internal confluence design page (batching-flush-design-v2).

End of notes — this is a working doc, will iterate into a playbook after we lock parameters and add regression tests.
